review: I know this almost goes without saying, but any gamer alive should play the Half-Life games. Even compared with the modern flashy big-budget single-player shooter extravaganzas of today (I'm looking at you, Far Cry and Bioshock), which are rightly heralded as amazing games, Half-Life makes your jaw drop at how amazing of an experience it is to fight throuth the crumbling Black Mesa facility battling humans and headcrabs alike. This game really makes you realize how much Jason Brody, Booker Dewitt, and every other major  fps protagonist since owe the man with the crowbar, Gordon Freeman. If you are a sane human being who can play a video game, there is no excuse for you to not play Half-Life. None!

This is an official "remake" of Half-Life. I use the word "remake" loosely because it's just a port of the original Half-Life built in Half-Life 2's Source Engine. Which in theory should be a good thing, an older game rebuilt in a newer game engine. Except instead of remaking the game properly Valve went about it in the laziest way possible. They just took the assets from Half-Life and dumped them into the Source engine. There's no real BIG difference between the two. But there are small differences between the two, most of which are bad.

There are some improvement from the original Half-Life that I can see. The enemies have rag doll physics. Some of the textures look slightly less muddy and the main menu has dynamic backgrounds like Half-Life 2 instead of just a JPG like in the original Half-Life. They used the Source Engine's dynamic lighting and particle effect system. Also some of the out door areas  have actual sky boxes instead of the low pixel still images the original game did. The water effects look better and the flashlight has a real time shadow effect now. Friendly NPC's AI has seen some noticeable improvements. While your escorting them it's harder for them to get lost.

However the issue is the game is noticeably buggy. Some bugs are bad enough that they do hurt the over all quality.

The ones I found are as follows.....

1. There's some screen tearing in a few places.

2. Some of the sound effects are... off. And that's because some of the sound effects have been removed and replaced with sound effects from Half-Life 2. Some of the sound effects were removed and replaced with nothing, making it so there's dead silence when some sound should be present. Some sound effects have been replaced with others, for example when you hit a wooden crate with your crowbar it's supposed to make that sound effect play but instead it plays the sound of you hitting a metal surface instead. No matter what surface you hit with your crowbar it will make the metal hitting sound effect, unless you hit an enemy. It's a lot louder and more ear piercing then most of the other sound effects which got on my nerves after a while. Seeing as you need to keep smashing wooden crates to get to the supplies inside.

3. The barnacle enemy's tongues don't always reach all the way down to the floor. Making it so they look like they're inactive but you'll get grabbed anyway. It's supper annoying that you can get grabbed and pulled up to ceiling after walking into nothing. There's also a section early on where the barnacle's are hidden behind some ceiling panels in a break room and their tongues clip through them. Making it so you can see them when your not supposed to.

4. There are times when the improved textures hurt the game rather that help it. Some areas are supposed to look dirty and trashed with blood stains and trash everywhere. But these areas look clean and spotless instead.

5. The weapon model on your magnum revolver looks weirdly shiny for some reason.

6. The MP5 has some weird sway effect now for some reason and dose way more damage. That includes when other people are using it, not just you.

7. If there's music playing when you hit a loading screen it'll just cut out when the loading screen ends.

8. If the security guard NPC's get injured while your escorting them they'll keep making that "oof" noise over and over again as if they're constantly getting injured.

9. There's this tentacle enemy you encounter in a few places like the blast pit in the rocket testing facility. This enemy is totally broken and can't deal any damage what so ever. The tentacles just clip right through you. Making it so you can just ignore them in every encounter.

10. The boss fight in Gonarch's Lair is kinda gimped. She won't attack you properly and instead will just stand around firing acid at you. When the acid hits the ground it will leave a black square shaped decal. 

11. During the mission Surface Tension the helicopter fight on the side of the cliff is broken too. The game doesn't give you enough rockets to shoot the helicopter down. So you'll be forced to use your other weapons to finish the job.

12. During the mission We Got Hostels in the original game there's a marine that kills a scientist but now that same marine dose nothing. This ruins a major story moment.

These are just the bugs I noticed while playing through the game once. There's some videos on YouTube by someone named Defenestrum that go into more detail.

All the improvements that Half-Life: Source makes to the original Half-Life game don't effect the game play all that much but all the things it dose worse dose effect the game play. Which is why I don't recommend playing this over the original. But there are two final nails in the coffin for me on this so called "remake"

The first one is that this version doesn't work with mods. The second is that there's now a real fan remake of Half-Life in the Source Engine called Black Mesa that's available here on Steam. So there doesn't seem to be much of a point in playing this or even for it to exist at all.

I'll give Half-Life: Source a Bethesda treatment out of 10

Half-Life Source is developed by Valve and released in 2004.
This is the Source Engine port of the first Half-Life,
originally using the GoldSrc engine and released in 1998.

Half-Life is a masterpiece of the FPS genre, 
unanimously acclaimed by players and the specialized press.
You can also read my review of Valve's first game [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/AymericTheNightmare/recommended/70?snr=1_5_9__402]here[/url].
Half-Life Source was billed as a remastered version of the 1998 title,
with updated graphics and improved physics.
If HL:S is fun to play, just like the original game that is great,
however, things need to be clarified from the start:
the Source Engine brings anecdotal new features to Half-Life,
and the game is riddled with an incalculable amount of bugs,
especially since the 2013 SteamPipe update.
Let's say that Half-Life Source is not inherently bad,
but it's clearly not the best version of Half-Life 1 either.

I'm going to do my best to try to explain in detail,
what makes Half-Life Source such an unique game.

The graphics are unchanged with identical textures, 
but slightly brighter than the original GoldSrc maps, 
due to the new light effects provided by the Source engine. Despite this, many places are quite dark and dull.
Half-Life 2's skybox system provides a little more realism, compared to the simple pixelated sky textures of the past.
Those of the "Surface Tension" levels are quite pretty, especially in the "c2a5a" map of "Surface Tension" (the cliff, with the Valve Theme). 
The water is much more detailed as well, but contrasts with the game's outdated graphics.

NPCs have ragdoll physics when they die.
If this is supposed to be more realistic, thanks to the Havok physics engine, 
this often gives rise to funny situations because of the angular models of the characters.
Unfortunately, it is no longer possible to explode corpses.
Too bad for those like me who love to stain all the places they visit with blood...

The characters, the creature, the H.E.V Suit, 
and the weapon models are more detailed with high-resolution textures.
They resemble the models from the High Definition Pack that came with Blue Shift and those from the PS2 version, both created by Gearbox Software.
But what many don't know is that Valve chose unofficial models for HL:S from a fan-made mod, called "High Definition Source" created by a man named Denisov in 2006...
The movements are clumsy, as are the fights.
Some weapons suffer from exaggerated recoil, like the Beretta pistol and the M16.
The C4 throw has a ridiculously low range, making this explosive almost useless.
We actually pick up the Snarks themselves rather than their nest.
Apache Helicopters fire the same rockets as Half-Life 2's APCs and Hunter-Choppers.
The impact effects are different, and change depending on the surface you shoot at.

This Source version of Half-Life is famous for its plethora of bugs and problems of all kinds.
Here are the many mperfections that I noticed while playing…

Several sounds are missing, such as reloading certain weapons, or scripted sounds.
The music reboots after each loading of "Black Mesa Inbound".
Others are cut off because of level transitions, for example in "We've Got Hostiles" or "On a Rail"! There are spawn bugs, like items floating, and a scientist levitating above his chair in the "c1a0b" map ("Anomalous Materials"). When I play the game in French, the voices of the H.E.C.U. Soldiers. remain in English, except in a few scripts in "On A Rail".
In this same chapter, in the map "c2a2g", the sniper entrenched high up is harmless, he does'nt shoot.
NPCs constantly repeat themselves when injured, 
while others are as mute as Gordon Freeman.
In the maps "c1a4i" ("Blast Pit"), "c2a5x" ("Surface Tension") and "c4a1b" ("Interloper"), Tentacles are harmless.
The electrified water of "c1a4f" from "Blast Pit" is invisible.
The Barnacles' tongue is not displayed correctly in some rooms, you can get trapped if you are incautious.
The "c2a4c" level of "Residue Processing" has terrible bright, colorful and psychedelic display bugs (see [url=https://youtu.be/o0cvPIdJdw4]here[/url] and [url=https://youtu.be/iCTf7zejoU0]there[/url]), worthy of an acid trip.
On Xen, when Gonarch spits his whitish substance onto the ground, a large black square texture appears.
Even though I've already encountered the bug where Gonarch stays on his web despite receiving damage, I didn't get it while writing this review.
In short, the list of bugs is endless, and I may have forgotten to note some…
And I consider myself lucky enough not to have suffered certain bugs that I read or saw on the internet...

So, is Half-Life Source a bad game?
Of course not, but its quality is clearly lower than its predecessor.
The game is often mocked, even ridiculed, by fans of the franchise.
The improvements made by the Source Engine are minor and only noticeable to veterans of the original game.
On the other hand, the bugs are legion and don't pay homage to either Half-Life or the Half-Life 2 engine.
For a large number of players, Half-Life Source turns out to be a port without much ambition on a new engine.
However, it is useful to Garry's Mod players thanks to its assets, and it's the same thing for Counter-Strike Source.
I was able to launch all the Half-Life Source maps in Counter-Strike Global Offensive, in my "CS:GO x HL1" project (see [url=https://youtu.be/AXm4kQpNP-Q]here[/url] and  [url=https://youtu.be/coQVlkT8BSs]there[/url]).
If it is true that the classic Half-Life at GoldSrc is undoubtedly the best version,
HL:S remains relatively pleasant to play and still has a certain charm.
You can have fun looking for little differences and bugs everywhere, if you feel like a beta tester.
But there is no point hoping for a possible future patch, the last big update dates back to 2013,
and it's this one which broke a good number of things in the game.
Worse still, Valve delisted the game during Half-Life's 25th anniversary, recognizing the original game as the definitive version.
So prefer the original Half-Life from 1998, cult in every way possible and technically impeccable.
Half-Life Source is nevertheless an interesting element of Valve's history, a game to be appreciated for its true value.
Keep in mind if you play it that it'is just a simple port from one engine to another.
It's not really a Remaster, and even less a Remake.
If you ever want to play a truly modernized version of Half-Life,
the talented and passionate developers of Crowbar Collective have created the excellent Black Mesa,
an excellent remake respecting the awesome original game while bringing a lot of great new features.
You can by the way read my review of Black Mesa [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/AymericTheNightmare/recommended/362890?snr=1_5_9__402]here[/url].

Would I recommend Half-Life? Hell yes. Would I recommend Half-Life: Source? Er, maybe. The original Half-Life was, and still is, an absolutely fantastic game. The story and how it’s conveyed to the player works extremely well, and the controls, gameplay mechanics, visuals, and sound are all phenomenal. Very few bugs, and certainly none game-breakingly noteworthy.

However, this is where Half-Life: Source fails. This game’s major problem is its glitches and bugs. Some minor, some absolutely game-breaking. On one hand, you have scientist’s AI screwed up, running into open fire, constantly shooting off their response lines. On the other hand, you have some parts of the game where the textures and models go apeshit, essentially simulating your graphics card melting.

Even with the bugs, the game does try to make it up with some enhancements thanks to the Source engine. The water effects are slightly better (although in my experiences it’s just extraordinarily shiny and reflective), and the lighting effects are significantly improved, although inconsistent when walking into an area that needs to load. However, the HL2 bullet hole decals make it possible to create magnificent works of art with your crowbar on walls. 

Thankfully, the gameplay, controls, and overall look and appeal of the game is still there, unaltered. There’s no denying that the game is awesome. Half-Life in general is awesome. I just love how people on the GoldSrc version of Half-Life were complaining about the game having extremely old and outdated graphics, saying HL:Source is better in this field. Well, it’s not. A majority of textures and models are completely identical. Aside from the water and bullet decals, the games are visually the same, which is something I’m completely fine with. The regular version of Half-Life actually comes with the HD texture pack, something this port lacks. It essentially gives the game updated models to characters and weapons, and slightly enhanced textures in some areas. It’s nice, but not essential, which is fine.

Overall, yeah, go ahead and get it. If this is ever on sale for cheaper than the regular Half-Life, and you own neither, by all means, go ahead and get it. You (hopefully) won’t regret it.

Yeah this is just the first Half-Life, but worse. It's an amazing game, just the worst version of that game. Instead of just saying that though, I'll give you a list of fair comparisons between this game and the original Half-Life.

Pros:
• The flashlight is way better
• Ragdolls are a lot of fun and the crossbow even pins them to walls
• The suit battery you gain before the resonance cascade remains after it happens
• A few effects are pretty cool, especially the blood splatters and bullets
• The section were the crates are hanging is more interesting due to the physics
• The scene where the tentacle drags the scientist out of the window looks way better
• The graphical overhaul looks nice in very specific circumstances

Cons:
• FULL of bugs
• Most new effects or graphical "improvements" look awful and clash with the original game's aesthetic
• Movement is floatier than the original game for no reason
• The game defaults to "Easy" difficulty
• The new weapon recoil is awful and makes most weapons harder to use (especially the MP5)
• C4 throwing distance is reduced to almost nothing

Half-Life: Source is the 2004 port of Valve's award winning game to the Source Engine. With just that knowledge, it would sound like Half-Life: Source was a gift from above, but it's anything BUT that. Half-Life: Source was critically panned, which makes you wonder HOW it has a "Very Positive" on Steam Reviews. Half-Life: Source is one of those games Valve chooses to forget, with the likes of the first Left 4 Dead and Ricochet. But, before we get into a review, lets go over the history of Half-Life: Source.

[h1]The History:[/h1]
In 1999, Valve started development of Half-Life 2, the award winning squeal to Half-Life, originally running on the GoldSource engine. Around 2001/2002, the Source Engine was created, and it surpassed what the GoldSource engine could do, so, Valve planned to port Half-Life to the Source Engine to have it replace the GoldSource counter parts. In 2003, Axel Gambe got a hold of the full Half-Life 2 Source Code, raw map data, and a build of Half-Life 2, who later gave it to some friends, who leaked it. In those leak files, there was the Half-Life Source port, along with files to a Source port of TFC, DMC, and CS 1.6 (which was remotely playable, but at this time, this port was starting to become the game we know today as CS:S.) The port of Half-Life: Source was quite buggy and unfinished, which is to be expected for it being a leak of a beta. So, 2004 comes around, and then Half-Life 2 is coming around the corner, as a bundle with Half-Life 2, you could get Counter-Strike: Source (by this time is the game we all know and probably love) and Half-Life: Source. Half-Life: Source saw little change from the 2003 leak of Half-Life 2, minus some minor bug fixes and having the Half-Life 1 HUD. At this point, be expected Half-Life: Source to be just like Counter-Strike: Source, a re-imagining of the game, in HD (for 2004 standards), but what they got was a direct Half-Life port that didn't seam quite finished. This is why if you ask anyone why they don't like Half-Life: Source for the most part (especially pre-2013) you get told it's graphics were just the Half-Life graphics. But as stated before, Half-Life: Source was meant to replace Half-Life as a whole, but due to how poorly received it was, Half-Life Original saw another day. In 2006, Valve ported the Deathmatch counter part of Half-Life into the Source Engine, and if you thought Half-Life: Source was a bad port, you should of saw this game. All player ragdolls had broken physics, some weapons were broken (the Shotgun's double barrel sound is just the single barrel sound), and the gameplay was more like Half-Life 2 Deathmatch with minor HLDM gameplay stuff slapped in (the game even lacks the backpack pickups that were in Half-Life Deathmatch), the only reason I can see for this port, was just to give EP1 a pack-in game. Around 2007, Half-Life: Source and Deathmatch: Source were ported to Source Base 2007, but due to the amount of bugs now included with the game, Valve didn't release this patch to the public, it wasn't until 2012 that the public knew of this update's existence, since in 2012, the whole 2008/2007 source code to Source Base 2007 was leaked into the public, it also confirmed that the Team Fortress Classic port was in further development than what everyone thought. But due to the amount of hate towards Half-Life: Source and Deathmatch: Source would mean we would probably never seen of these ports.

So, that runs down a good chunk of the history of Half-Life: Source besides one of the more major things, the 2013 update. Valve in an effort to ditch the GCF system and upgrade everything to VPK and have a better downloading system and a better game asset pack to engine communication, they created Steampipe, but since Valve decided it would be best to port all games to Source Base 2013, they decided to do that, and try to provide updates to all Valve games. In the same year, Valve canned the project, leaving a ton of games in a broken state, Half-Life: Source being one of them.

So, this leads us into the review.

[H1]The Review[/h1]
Half-Life: Source was a mediocre port to the Source Engine, where it would be mixed who liked the game and disliked the game, since Half-Life: Source had that audience. Half-Life: Source is now a BAD port to the Source Engine, since those 2013 updates broke more than what it fixed. Not only did Valve cancel the updates to these games, they released the beta depots into the release depot to remove traces of GCFs. So, those games that had a good release depot, now have a beta released into them, and a lot of these betas were far from done. We now have broken Save/Restore errors in various NPCs, 2 out of the 3 tentacles in Blast Pit can harm the player or AI, one of the maps in Residue Processing will blind the player if your flashlight is turned on, skill configurations are broken (so now the AI is harder), Gonarch spit is now black squares, one of the maps in Surface Tension has a broken skybox, you can jump over a lot of things making it so you can skip half of "We got Hostiles" and skip various other parts in other chapters, all of the Chrome shaders are complete ass (they were never good, but this is just worse), and even more. It's sad when a 2003 leak is better and more playable than a 2013 update. Plus, if you load the HD Pack you get a GameBanana skin pack, since Valve was too lazy to port the assets their selves of even double check to be everything matched in the first place. But the icing on the cake is that, well, at first install, you can't even PLAY Half-Life: Source since Valve provided corrupted or outdated DLLs to Steam VR, so every time you reinstall Half-Life: Source you have to verify the cache of Half-Life 2 or Steam VR. Not only that, the person who was working on these updates, Alfred, shrugged off a few errors as design points.

Half-Life: Source had potential to be a great port, to even be on par with the Original Half-Life (definitely should NEVER replace the Original), but its potential was lost with a company who couldn't care enough about the game, which is why it was left for about 6 years without an update.

I recommend to play Half-Life: Source and Deathmatch: Source so you can see what happens when a company just flat out doesn't give a fucking shit.

Half-Life: Source, released in 2004 by Valve, is an enhanced version of the original 1998 masterpiece, running on the Source engine. While it aimed to improve the visuals, physics, and water effects, it failed to live up to expectations, making it a divisive version among fans.

Despite still delivering the legendary Half-Life experience, this remaster feels more like a rushed port than a true upgrade.

What Works Well?
🧪 Same Brilliant Gameplay as Half-Life
At its core, Half-Life: Source is still Half-Life—one of the most influential FPS games ever made. The engaging story, immersive atmosphere, and smart enemy AI remain intact, making this version playable and enjoyable.

🌊 Improved Water Effects and Physics
The transition to the Source engine brings better physics (thanks to Havok) and improved water reflections, which make certain areas look more modern compared to the 1998 original.

🖥️ Smoother Performance and Native Support
Half-Life: Source runs natively on modern systems, avoiding the compatibility issues that can arise with the original GoldSrc version. Higher resolutions and widescreen support are also a plus.

The Problems with Half-Life: Source
❌ Barely Any Real Graphical Upgrade
Despite running on Source, most textures, models, and lighting effects remain unchanged from 1998. This makes it feel less like a true remaster and more like a basic port with minimal effort.

❌ Buggy AI and Broken Scripted Sequences
Some of Half-Life’s iconic scripted moments don’t work properly in Half-Life: Source, breaking immersion. Enemies and NPCs sometimes behave worse than in the original, which is unacceptable for an "improved" version.

❌ No High-Definition (HD) Model Pack
Unlike Half-Life’s official 1999 update, which introduced better character and weapon models, Half-Life: Source lacks these HD assets—making it feel graphically inferior to an older update of the game.

❌ Black Mesa Exists
If you want to experience Half-Life with Source engine upgrades, Black Mesa (a fan-made, Valve-approved remake) is a far superior alternative with fully reworked graphics, animations, and improved gameplay mechanics.

Conclusion
Half-Life: Source is not a bad way to play Half-Life, but it's also not the best. If you want the original experience, the GoldSrc version is more authentic. If you want a true Source engine remake, Black Mesa is the better choice.

[i]Half-Life[/i] is one of my all-time favourite games, to be sure.  When I first played it back in 1998, it instantly became my standard for all shooters thereafter.

So why wouldn't I recommend this version?  True, it might make playing the older game more palatable to someone accustomed to the much more technically sophisticated games of today, without resorting to the outright remake that is [i]Black Mesa[/i].  But, sadly,  [i]Half-Life: Source[/i] is notoriously buggy.  It seems that transplanting the game onto the new physics engine spawned a remarkable number of new problems.  Curiously, Valve does not seem interested in addressing them, and given the time that has passed, seems unlikely to ever do so.

I've seen a number of presentations, on Youtube and the like, and in print, that list the great many bugs and glitches and whatnot that plague [i]Half-Life: Source[/i], and have also heard people report that they had no problem with it at all.  So I decided to see for myself what, if any, I might personally encounter in my own test run of the game.

The results:
[olist]
[*]Any time a friendly NPC is injured, he continues to cry out at irregular intervals as though being injured over and over again.  Minor, but very irritating when you have the NPC (or NPCs) following you around for any length of time.
[*]BLAST PIT (SPOILERS):  [spoiler]The blast pit, uh, "kraken", is apparently incapable of inflicting damage.  There is absolutely no challenge to this part of the map.  In fact, no kraken anywhere (e.g. on the surface, in Xen) can inflict damage.  You can simply waltz right by it as it thrashes at you ineffectually.  A first-time player would be baffled by its inclusion and would miss out on one of the more original and bizarre "boss" encounters ever devised in a shooter.  Utterly pointless.[/spoiler]
[*]Boss Fights (SPOILERish): [spoiler]This may or may not be a bug, but I noticed that the Gluon gun was worthless in all boss fights, and RPGs in particular against the Gonarch.  I ended up killing the Gonarch with the shotgun, of all things.  Now, it may be that the weapons were deliberately rebalanced for this version of the game.  After all, I did prevail.  But I have noticed others complain about similar issues, so I thought it worth mentioning.[/spoiler]
[*]Ending (Again, SPOILERS):  [spoiler]The G-Man is mute!  He just stands there, mouth unmoving, looking at you/Gordon, occasionally gesturing during the scenery changes.  Finally, he just stands near the open train car door, waiting.  Who knows what a first-time player would make of this?  Baffling, '2001'-style surrealism?  Leaving this unfixed merits a face-palm...[/spoiler]
[/olist]
Suffice it to say, whether or not you have read the spoilers, the bugs in my version of the game injure the experience of the game in two significant ways.  One robs the game of one of its signature challenges, and the other ruins a key character and iconic story moment.  I would say it's too great a cost for the improved graphics and physics, especially for someone playing the game for the first time.   The original game is cleaned up and pleasing enough to the eye, and retains its "retro" charm for those interested in that aspect of it.  More importantly, it works!  Meanwhile, the excellent [i]Black Mesa[/i] actually succeeds in updating the old game to [i]Half-Life 2[/i] standards (and then some).  Play the latter game with the Update mod and you'd think they were two chapters of the same game, more or less. 

Given the above options, and the current state of poor-old neglected [i]Half-Life: Source[/i], I can barely recommend it even as a curiosity to [i]Half-Life[/i] or Valve completists.  The only reason I have it is because it came with the bundle...

I will give it one BIG positive over the original [i]Half-Life[/i], though:  It is a LOT easier to herd friendly NPCs, and you can at some points in the game have a small army of security guards (i.e. 'Barneys') following you around.  Just don't be standing in front of them if a head crab drops down from the ceiling...


[b]TLDR:[/b]  If you have never played [i]Half-Life[/i] before, don't play this version.  If you have, either apply a reputable bug-fixing mod or just play [i]Black Mesa[/i] instead.  

[b]UPDATE:[/b]  It has recently occurred to me that I own several games that are buggy messes "out of the box", or have compatibility issues, especially with @%&!*#$ Windows 10.  I have had great pleasure in modding/fixing these games to workable and often improved states, and would probably still recommend them (albeit with caveats). So why single out [i]HL: Source[/i]?

I suppose it is because I expect Valve to be as dedicated to the quality and stability of this game as they are with the rest of their products, including the "original" [i]Half-Life[/i], and the issues I have described above are too high a price to pay for the cosmetic improvements gained.  Listed in the Guides folder for this game are some comprehensive bug-fixing mods that very likely deal with all of the issues I have personally experienced, and probably a lot more.   A successful test of one of these may well reverse my non-recommendation.

Valve really came ahead of the bunch, releasing a remaster of an older a game, porting assets to a newer, more capable and robust engine, before remasters became a thing. The idea is great on paper, but in reality it turned out messy, and I'm being polite here. You can watch reviews online on why that is and why you should not touch this game even with a 10 foot pole.

But what if I told you that you can actually play it and not suffer from all those issues? Thanks to a "Fixed" mod, the game is somewhat glitch-free, apart from some stuff (the mod has a document of issues that were not fixed). The game has crashed on me 3-4 times (not much more than the original does for me) and there was one time that my save got corrupted, but since I do quick saves all the time, that was not a big deal. I also did not read the document about what's not fixed, so I had the most raw possible experience.

Let's talk positive. The game looks genuinely nicer! It feels like the game was not released in 1998, more like 2001, maybe 2002. New water and particle effects stand out especially. Some of the environments look much more vibrant, lively and even natural (especially the canyon section). The Source engine also introduced ragdoll physics, which makes the game feel much newer, too, but you can still blow up people like you used to in the original. I played with HD models enabled (which I might get shot for doing so), but you can always disable them, if you wanted to (requires a restart, sadly). Some of the models were given a visual quality bump, it feels like. Grenades actually look like grenades, M16 looks darker and the revolver is not shiny like it was left out in polishing for decades. Everything looks subtly better, and you will mostly notice differences when played side by side with original game or if you've played the original a bunch of times.

Now, the negatives/issues. Mind you, I played the game on hardest difficulty, so some of the issues seemed more pronounced because of that. First of all, the elephant in the room, the SMG/M16. The "camera shake" is still present, but the gun seem to be a bit more accurate to compensate for that. If you are not aware, during longer bursts, for some reason, Valve decided to artificially add recoil to the gun, which makes your camera go up and down in unpredictable manner. First of all, why up and... DOWN? It would be easier to compensate for if it was going only up, even more so if it was predictable. It's just all over the place.

It seems like some of the scripted scenes are still mildly broken. They feel like they are delayed for couple of seconds, for some reason, and NPC's (both hostile and friendly) seem to react to your presence when they shouldn't.

Now let's talk combat. First of all, enemies are all bullet sponges (hard difficulty, duh), but since when marines can take a crossbow bolt without dying? Same for vorts, actually. Houndeyes have broken hitboxes (don't even try hitting anything other than eyes) and controllers are the worst offenders. For some reason, once they see you, they will instantly start flying to you head on, which they didn't do in original. That took me of guard, but I kept playing, since I could take a difficulty spike like this, even though the game felt substantially harder (I was almos always out of something: be it ammo or health and/or HEV suit charge). What I couldn't take is how broken the hitboxes were on both Gonarch and Nihilanth. Both took all almost all my ammo to kill and made me resort to hivehand, which, by the way, still restores ammo while holstered, but you get +1 ammo icon every time it restores when you're holding it and, when you holster it while not full and you're not holding it, you will only get full ammo ~1 second after you get it back from the inventory, showing you the amount of ammo you left it with. Jank.

Back to Xen bosses. They almost made me pull my hair out, they took me much more time than they used to in original, even on Hard. During Nihilanth I actually took the portals to get the ammo necessary to kill him (which I almost never do, since I have enough before the fight anyway), and never in my life I though that the way to finish him is to throw a C4 into his head and blow it up (never did that in my life, firing from the ground was always enough before).

These are the issues that came from the top of my head as more memorable ones. There are couple more little quirks I have forgotten because of how insignifficant they were, but they are still there, nonetheless.

In conclusion, even with the mod, the game is more of a novelty, really, an answer to a "What if?" question.  I still enjoyed all of the game, Half Life is still Half Life, even if you give it couple of crowbar hits. If you prefer more glitchless experience and don't mind a bit older graphics, play the original. If you are fine with some bugs, crashes and glitches and prefer a bit better looking image overall, play HL: Source with a "Fixed" mod. Recommended.

Psst, if you want to experience an amazing-looking Half Life experience on newer Source engine, without the glitches and with MUCH better graphics? Look no further than Black Mesa. It's an awesome remake made by fans, which was actually made in response to Half Life: Source and how badly made it was.
It may be a bit broken but it is fun to play and use in Garrys mod.

On the one hand, they added ragdoll physics, and corpses now fall naturally rather than animatedly, water now shimmers, dynamic shadows have appeared, the interface has been redesigned to match the style of the second game, and the menus are now more user-friendly. But that's where the positives end. The version is terribly crude, and although I did encounter some bugs, they weren't critical, but still. In some places, the developers even simplified the levels, which I didn't notice. I'm not a huge fan, but it's still disappointing. I wouldn't be so categorical, and I don't see the point in giving it a negative rating. It's more of a showcase for the capabilities of the new Source engine.

Half-Life: Source is more of a novelty or a tech demo rather than a full polished release. It was released after the infamous Valve leaks and before the release of Half-Life 2, which most likely caused it to be rushed. As a result, Half-Life: Source is extremely buggy and has some "graphical enhancements" which are mostly downgrades from the original game. The new "HD models" aren't great, the floors are shiny for some reason, and the water looks really bad.

In fact, some of the "HD models" were actually ripped from [url=https://gamebanana.com/mods/239219]GameBanana[/url] and [url=https://www.reddit.com/r/HalfLife/comments/f62gub/halflife_sources_hd_models_are_fanmade/]weren't even made by Valve[/url] at all. If you look at the [url=https://imgur.com/SvpBszC]HEV suit's arm texture,[/url] you can see the fan artists signature.

There's almost no reason to play this over the original, unless you really enjoy the novelty of Half-Life being in the Source engine. If you want Half-Life with better graphics, then [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/362890/Black_Mesa/]Black Mesa[/url] is a much better option.
